title: Ontario Wildfires Grow to 1.8 Million Acres as Smoke Chokes US Midwest
excerpt: Nearly 200 active blazes are burning across Ontario as wildfire smoke continues to trigger unhealthy air quality alerts across the US Midwest, stoking tensions between Washington and Ottawa.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ontario wildfires have expanded to 1.8 million acres with 190 active blazes and 1,800 residents evacuated.
  • US Midwest air quality is rated 'unhealthy' in several states due to smoke from the wildfires.
  • President Trump criticized Canada's wildfire response, threatening tariffs amid escalating US-Canada tensions.
  • The Collins First Nation community was destroyed, forcing residents to evacuate by boat with nothing left.

Data from Ontario Premier Doug Ford and local reports.
  • Ontario wildfires have expanded to 735,000 hectares (1.8 million acres), with 190 active blazes burning across the province and approximately 1,800 residents evacuated.
  • Air quality in the US Midwest remains rated "unhealthy" across parts of Wisconsin, Iowa, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Michigan.
  • President Trump has criticised Canada's wildfire response and threatened tariffs, while Canadian PM Mark Carney has said all countries must do more on climate change.
  • The fires destroyed the Collins First Nation (Namaygoosisagagun) community, forcing residents to flee by boat with nothing remaining.

The Scale of the Crisis

Wildfires burning across Ontario have grown to 735,000 hectares — roughly 1.8 million acres — from 650,000 hectares over the weekend, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said at a press conference in Toronto on Monday. The province is battling 190 active blazes, mostly in remote, difficult-to-access areas of northwestern Ontario, with around 1,800 residents evacuated from sparsely populated communities.

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2079292760599957904

"We will not spare a penny fighting these fires and keeping people safe," Ford said, according to Reuters.

> **""There was nothing remaining," incident commander Matthew Hoppe told Reuters."**

""There was nothing remaining," incident commander Matthew Hoppe told Reuters."

The destruction has been devastating in some communities. Fire destroyed the Namaygoosisagagun First Nation, also known as Collins First Nation, forcing residents to flee by boat. "There was nothing remaining," incident commander Matthew Hoppe told Reuters. Thunder Bay is at full capacity sheltering evacuees, Mayor Ken Boshcoff said, while reports indicate that more than 30 homes were lost in Collins.

Smoke Reaches Deep Into the United States

Heavy smoke from the fires in northern and western Ontario, combined with blazes in northern Minnesota, has created some of the worst air quality readings on the planet. Last week, Toronto recorded the world's worst air quality. The smoke has since spread to New York and Washington before settling over the Midwest.

As of Monday morning, the US Environmental Protection Agency's AirNow site rated air quality as "unhealthy" or "unhealthy for sensitive groups" across parts of Wisconsin, Iowa, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Michigan. Health officials warn that wildfire smoke contains fine particulate matter (PM2.5) that can worsen asthma, heart disease and other respiratory conditions.

US-Canada Tensions Escalate

The wildfires have become a diplomatic flashpoint. President Trump said he spoke to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney about the issue at the FIFA World Cup final, two days after threatening tariffs on Canadian goods to punish Canada over the wildfire smoke. Carney has not directly responded to Trump's criticism, though he has said all countries, including the United States, must do more to address climate change.

Michigan Republicans have joined the criticism of Canada's fire management. Canadian commentators have pushed back, noting that no country could strip combustible material from forests on Canada's scale.

Climate Context

Canada has reported about 3,500 wildfires in 2026, close to its recent five-year average. However, the number of simultaneously active fires — 859 across the country as of mid-July — remains exceptionally high. The total area burned nationally sits near 28,500 square kilometres, while in the US, roughly 3.7 million acres have burned, above the 10-year average of 2.7 million.

Diplomatic Tensions Rise
›Trump threatens tariffs over Canada's wildfire response.
›Carney emphasizes global climate responsibility.
›Michigan Republicans criticize Canada's fire management.

"As our climate warms, we're seeing more extreme weather, and we're going to see more fire," said Mike Flannigan, a wildland fire professor at Thompson Rivers University in British Columbia.

What to Watch

Thunderstorms are expected to bring some precipitation to fire zones, but forecasters caution that coverage will be uneven — some areas may get heavy rain while neighbouring areas remain dry. Until widespread, sustained rainfall develops, fire activity and cross-border smoke are expected to continue. For the millions of people affected by poor air quality across both countries, the advice remains to limit outdoor activity, exercise indoors and keep windows closed.
